newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian opposition party calls for change.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian opposition party calls for change.

text.p: A congress of Hungary's opposition party Fidesz called for the replacement of the Socialist-Liberal government.
Fidesz said corruption was becoming more widespread, average living standards had fallen sharply, and the government's policies did not ensure sustainable economic growth.

"The theses approved by the congress may become the basis of the programme of a new civic government to be set up following the 1998 elections," Fidesz' vice president Tamas Deutsch told a news conference following the week-end party congress.
Fidesz is the only party in the Hungarian parliament which has not been a member of a government since the fall of the Communist regime in 1990.
Fidesz and another opposition party, the Smallholders, are running neck and neck in opinion polls ahead of the Socialists, the senior governing party.
Support for the Socialists has been hit by a fall in real wages of about 15 percent in the past two years and a corruption scandal at the state privatisation agency in 1996.
"The governing left wing parties have weakened substantially and their support has halved since the 1994 election," Fidesz vice president Janos Ader said.

Fidesz said a right wing government would crack down on corruption, narrow the gap between the rich and the poor and create sustainable economic growth by encouraging investments, cutting taxes and supporting small companies.
The government has an economic growth target of three percent this year and four to five percent in 1998.
But an austerity programme launched in 1995 has suppressed growth and a rapid increase in the trade deficit was likely this year, Fidesz said.
Deutsch said a Fidesz-led government would freeze the privatisation oil and gas company MOL, electricity company MVM, broadcaster Antenna Hungaria and airline Malev.

Fidesz agrees with the government that Hungary should join NATO and the European Union (EU). But it must fight harder for its interests in future talks with the EU than it has done so far, Fidesz said.
